Indeed, a leader of the [[Ogron Confederation of Planets]] was unfamiliar with the Daleks. ([[COMIC]]: ''[[The Lost Dimension (comic story)|The Lost Dimension]]'')

The [[Skaro Degradations]] were Daleks from [[Parallel universe|alternate universes]] whose creation points had been intercepted by the Daleks of N-Space. They were used by the N-Space Daleks during the [[Last Great Time War]]. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Engines of War (novel)}})

Using the powers of the [[quantum harvester]], [[Dorothy Bell]] once observed a parallel universe where the Tenth Doctor was chased by a Dalek heavily resembling an [[Egypt]]ian [[sarcophagus]]. ([[COMIC]]: ''[[Old Girl (comic story)|Old Girl]]'')

In [[the Warrior's universe]], [[Sarah Jane Smith]] convinced [[The Warrior|the Doctor]] to destroy the incubation chamber only for an already active [[prototype]] Dalek to both kill her and [[Harry Sullivan]] and fatally wound the Doctor, only for him to transported back to Gallifrey before it could deal the killing blow. Enduring despite the Doctor's actions, the Daleks discovered the abandoned [[Fourth Doctor's Time Ring|Time Ring]]. Joining with the Kaleds and Thals, the Daleks became part of the [[Unified Skaroan Alliance]] and reverse engineered the [[Time Ring]] to become a temporal power, waging a [[time war]] against [[Gallifrey]]. ([[AUDIO]]: ''[[Dust Devil (audio story)|Dust Devil]]'', ''[[Aftershocks (audio story)|Aftershocks]]'')

== Society and culture ==
=== Overview ===
The Daleks were best-known as a warlike race who waged war across whole civilisations and with races all over the universe. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Daleks (TV story)}}, {{cs|Doomsday (TV story)}}) When the [[Eleventh Doctor]] was on the [[Dalek Asylum]] he considered the Daleks the most advanced [[warrior race]] in the universe, ([[TV]]: {{cs|Asylum of the Daleks (TV story)}}) and the [[Twelfth Doctor]] later concurred that the middle of a Dalek war zone was the deadliest place he knew. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Pilot (TV story)}})

=== Appreciation of beauty ===
Although Daleks proudly proclaimed that they had "no concept of elegance" ([[TV]]: {{cs|Doomsday (TV story)}}) and the [[One in a Million Dalek]]'s willingness to protect the perishable beauty of flowers was seen as an aberration by his [[Dalek Prime|Emperor]], ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|Shadow of Humanity (comic story)}}) the [[Thal]]s knew that the Daleks' forefathers had been "great thinkers and philosophers". ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Daleks (TV story)}}) Though they did not sing, ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|Jubilee (audio story)}}) the Daleks were still known to write poetry. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|The Also People (novel)}}) Some of the more elaborate Dalek battle cries had an almost poetic quality about them (for example, "Advance and Attack! Attack and Destroy! Destroy and Rejoice!") ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Chase (TV story)}}) and repetition of words such as "Predict! Predict! Predict!" ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Parting of the Ways (TV story)}}) and "Explain! Explain! Explain! ([[TV]]: {{cs|Journey's End (TV story)}})

As a means of [[entertainment]], the ''Dalek Survival Guide'' claimed that the Daleks occasionally enjoyed watching [[re-run]]s of great Dalek [[victory|victories]], but stated that their true [[passion]] was for [[reconnaissance]]; a Dalek would go to any lengths to gather new [[information]], and they would often put themselves at great risk to do so. The guide presented an image of a Dalek using its [[sucker arm]] to take a copy of ''[[The Complete Works of Shakespeare]]''; ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Dalek Survival Guide (novel)}}) in an [[alternate timeline]] where they ruled over Earth, the Daleks claimed to have a fondness for the works of [[William Shakespeare]], but the [[Eighth Doctor]] understood this to be a lie. ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|The Time of the Daleks (audio story)}}) According to a [[diary]] kept by a [[Time traveller (Time Traveller's Diary)|human time traveller]], the Daleks observed a holiday known as "[[Extermination Day]]" every other day. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Time Traveller's Diary (novel)}})

[[File:Daleks Awakening.jpg|left|thumb|Several [[Insanity|insane]] Daleks in the [[Dalek Asylum|asylum]], only kept alive because the rest of [[Resurrected Dalek Empire|the empire]] valued their hatred. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Asylum of the Daleks (TV story)}})]]
More "disgustingly" (in the words of the [[Eleventh Doctor]]), the Daleks viewed pure [[hate|hatred]] as beautiful and worth preserving even at a great cost, which was the reason for the existence of the [[Dalek Asylum]], where Daleks so blithely hateful that they presented a danger to their own people were kept. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Asylum of the Daleks (TV story)}}) Earlier in Dalek history, the [[Dalek Prime Strategist]] implemented a plan that defeated an entire [[Mechonoid]] army on Skaro. When the [[Emperor of the Restoration]] looked for a word to describe the plan, the Strategist suggested "effective," but the Emperor instead called it "beautiful." ([[WC]]: {{cs|Day of Reckoning (webcast)}})

The [[Tenth Doctor]] believed that [[music]] was "all just noise" to the Daleks, an observation which inspired him to temporarily repel a few Daleks by amplifying a radio's harmonies into a screech that was already painful to human ears, but seemed downright unbearable to the Daleks. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Evolution of the Daleks (TV story)}})

=== The Doctor ===
Due to their frequent defeats by the Doctor, he became a legendary figure in Dalek culture and mythology. They had standing orders to capture or exterminate the Doctor on sight, and were occasionally able to identify him despite his [[regeneration]]s. The Daleks knew the Doctor as the "[[Ka Faraq Gatri]]", meaning the "Bringer of Darkness" or "[[Destroyer of Worlds]]". ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|Bringer of Darkness (comic story)}}) Indeed, after the Doctor had shattered the Daleks' ambition to wipe out all of creation save for themselves using a [[reality bomb]], an enraged [[Davros]] screamed to the Doctor that he "named [him], ''forever'', the Destroyer of Worlds!!…". ([[TV]]: {{cs|Journey's End (TV story)}})

The [[Ninth Doctor]] told the human-born Daleks he met on [[Satellite Five]] that "the ancient legends of the Dalek homeworld" referred to him as "the Oncoming Storm". ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Parting of the Ways (TV story)}}) The Doctor was also referred to as the Predator of the Daleks. Shortly before the destruction of the Dalek Asylum, [[Clara Oswald#Oswin Oswald|Oswin]] erased all knowledge of the Doctor from every Dalek's memory. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Asylum of the Daleks (TV story)}}) However, the Daleks regained their memory of the Doctor from [[Tasha Lem]]. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Time of the Doctor (TV story)}}) Remembering their foe drove the [[Prime Minister of the Daleks]] insane. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Dalek: The Astounding Untold History of the Greatest Enemies of the Universe (short story)}})

[[File:ROTD greeneyestalk.jpg|thumb|right|The [[Seventh Doctor]] seen through a Dalek [[eyestalk]]. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Remembrance of the Daleks (TV story)}})]]
The Daleks had also been a vital part of the Doctor's growth, as he made it his mission to combat evil in the universe after meeting the Daleks during his [[First Doctor|First incarnation]]. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Into the Dalek (TV story)}}) Though the Doctor sometimes thought he had totally defeated his nemeses, the [[Tenth Doctor]] was angered by the belief that, while he would lose everything, the Daleks always survived. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Daleks in Manhattan (TV story)}}) After the years of combat between the time traveller and the Dalek race, Davros stated that the Doctor had "slaughtered" billions of Daleks. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Witch's Familiar (TV story)}})

The Daleks saw the Doctor as their greatest enemy. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Chase (TV story)}}, {{cs|Victory of the Daleks (TV story)}}, {{cs|Evolution of the Daleks (TV story)}}) Even though he once referred to [[the Master]] as his [[archenemy]], ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Deadly Assassin (TV story)}}) the Doctor also described the Daleks as his greatest foes ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|Defender of the Daleks (comic story)}}) and archenemies, going as far as to view them as the greatest sin in the universe. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Victory of the Daleks (TV story)}}) Similarly, during his [[Twelfth Doctor|Twelfth life]], the Doctor stated Davros, the creator of the Daleks, was his arch nemesis. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Magician's Apprentice (TV story)}}) When talking about the Daleks to [[Ace]], the [[Seventh Doctor]]'s voice developed a hard edge that unsettled her. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Illegal Alien (novel)}})

According to [[Clara Oswald]], the Doctor was scared of the Daleks, which made their companion's fear increase as well. ([[PROSE]]: ''[[The Companion's Companion (novel)|The Companion's Companion]]'') The [[War Doctor]] once reflected that he feared what the Daleks represented more than the Daleks themselves, ([[AUDIO]]: ''[[The Enigma Dimension (audio story)|The Enigma Dimension]]'') whereas the [[Ninth Doctor]] was mortified upon seeing a [[Metaltron|Dalek]] after the Time War, screaming in fear before relishing in its agony. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Dalek (TV story)}}) While talking with [[Rusty (Into the Dalek)|Rusty]], the Twelfth Doctor stated that, if he was helped in any way, the Daleks would be hurt. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Twice Upon a Time (TV story)}}) The [[Thirteenth Doctor]] stated that encounters with the Daleks were personal. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Resolution (TV story)}}) The Daleks did not make up part of the [[Fifth Doctor]]'s anti-[[Morbius]] [[The Alliance (Warmonger)|alliance]], but he had a nightmare where they offered their help. ([[PROSE]]: ''[[Warmonger (novel)|Warmonger]]'')

=== Psychology ===
Daleks had little individual personality and a strict hierarchy. They were conditioned to obey a superior's orders without question, even if these orders resulted in pain or death. ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|The Curse of Davros (audio story)}}) Indeed, [[Dalek Jast]] told a [[Dalek-human]] that Daleks did not [[question]] orders, ([[TV]]: {{cs|Evolution of the Daleks (TV story)}}) whilst [[Dalek Thay]] maintained that Daleks did not take orders from non-Daleks, ([[TV]]: {{cs|Doomsday (TV story)}}) with another Dalek stating that Daleks did not answer [[human]] [[question]]s. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Stolen Earth (TV story)}})

The most fundamental feature of Dalek culture and psychology was an unquestioned belief in the superiority of the Daleks. Other species were either to be exterminated or enslaved, and then exterminated when no longer necessary. The default directive of a Dalek was to destroy all non-Dalek life forms. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Power of the Daleks (TV story)}}, {{cs|Dalek (TV story)}}, et al.) They interestingly tended to project a similar mindset on other species; they found it difficult to understand that [[human]]s sometimes destroyed members of their own species, ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Power of the Daleks (TV story)}}) and several Daleks observed that there was something admirable about [[the Doctor]]'s hatred of the Daleks and intent to wipe them out completely, even if they found it monstrous that this exterminating intent was directed at them. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Dalek (TV story)}}, {{cs|Asylum of the Daleks (TV story)}}, {{cs|Into the Dalek (TV story)}})

Because of their belief in their species' superiority, ([[TV]]: {{cs|Daleks in Manhattan (TV story)}}) Daleks even regarded Daleks whose DNA deviated from their race's standard genetic makeup as their enemies and worthy of extermination, considering these deviant units impure. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Revolution of the Daleks (TV story)}}) [[Imperial-Renegade Dalek Civil War|The civil war]] between the [[Renegade Dalek|Renegade]] and [[Imperial Dalek]]s was an example of this. Each faction considered the other a perversion despite the relatively minor differences. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Remembrance of the Daleks (TV story)}}) This belief also meant that Daleks were intolerant of such "contamination" even within themselves. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Dalek (TV story)}}, {{cs|The Parting of the Ways (TV story)}}, {{cs|Evolution of the Daleks (TV story)}}, [[AUDIO]]: {{cs|The Mutant Phase (audio story)}}) Despite this, Daleks felt offended by exterminating their own "divine hatred", and deviant Daleks would sometimes instead be sent to the Dalek Asylum, should their hatred be deemed pure enough. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Asylum of the Daleks (TV story)}}) At other points in their history, however, they showed no hesitation to exterminating those they deemed impure. In fact, when a [[Reconnaissance Dalek|cloned recon Dalek]] noted it could be purified thanks to its remaining Dalek DNA, a [[Dalek leader (Revolution of the Daleks)|Dalek commander]] responded by ordering its destruction, proclaiming that extermination was the only purification the Daleks offered. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Revolution of the Daleks (TV story)}})

[[File:Normal Dalek 337.jpg|thumb|left|A Time War Dalek. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Dalek (TV story)}})]]
Another result of this superiority complex was their complete ruthlessness. This was due to genetic modifications made to the original Kaled mutants by Davros. It was because of this that it was nearly impossible to negotiate or reason with a Dalek, and it was this single-mindedness that made them so dangerous.

Their reliance on logic and machinery was a weakness, albeit one that they recognised. During the Movellan war, Daleks considered illogical actions impossible. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Destiny of the Daleks (TV story)}}) Later, one Dalek went out of its way to say its species did not rely on logic to make decisions, stating they instead relied on hatred and their own power, which it deemed to be superior sources of power. ([[GAME]]: ''[[Lost in Time (video game)/Events|All Aboard!]]'') The Daleks also transferred emotions from other life-forms in at least two instances, in one case humans, having refined the [[Human Factor]] with the help from the [[Second Doctor]] to create [[humanised Dalek]]s. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Evil of the Daleks (TV story)}}) In another instance, they refined slyness from the [[Xxarqon]], cruelty from the [[Tentrax]] and insane hatred from the [[Glarosus]]. ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|Doctor Who and the Dogs of Doom (comic story)}})

[[Metaltron|One unintentionally humanised Dalek]] occurred after it used [[Rose Tyler]]'s [[DNA]] to regenerate after sustaining injuries, involuntarily developing positive feelings. Its traditional Dalek psychology remained, however, and it ultimately self-destructed in disgust. The emotional capacity of Daleks was limited to largely negative emotions (hate being chief among them), as "human" emotions such as compassion and sentimentality were considered by them to be weaknesses. However, they were capable of comprehending these emotions, and often used them to exploit their enemies. A prime example occurred with the lone Dalek in [[Henry van Statten]]'s [[The Vault (Dalek)|vault]]; while talking with the [[Ninth Doctor]], the Dalek chose its words carefully, hoping to goad the [[Time Lord]] into initiating a physical attack on the chained mutant. Later, the Dalek played on an unwitting Rose Tyler's feelings of pity and compassion, leading her to touch its battered casing and restore energy to the near-dead Dalek. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Dalek (TV story)}})

Additionally, the Daleks used the greed of [[Theodore Maxtible]] to make him their ally. However, Daleks never formed permanent alliances; once their allies outlived their usefulness, they were usually exterminated on the spot. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Daleks' Master Plan (TV story)}}, {{cs|The Evil of the Daleks (TV story)}}, [[AUDIO]]: {{cs|The Mutant Phase (audio story)}}) A [[Death Squad Dalek]] claimed that Daleks did not need allies, ([[TV]]: {{cs|Revolution of the Daleks (TV story)}}) and a [[Type V Dalek|Exxilon Dalek]] claimed that Daleks did not require "the [[co-operation]] of inferior [[creature]]s." ([[TV]]: {{cs|Death to the Daleks (TV story)}})

The Ninth Doctor claimed that Daleks were incapable of any emotion except hate, ([[TV]]: {{cs|Dalek (TV story)}}) and later that they had "removed all [their] emotions", though he speculated there remained "one little spark" of [[fear]] somewhere in their DNA. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Parting of the Ways (TV story)}}) However, many Daleks were shown displaying a wider range of emotion, {{Gomez}} claimed that Daleks used emotions such as hate and anger to fuel their weapons. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Witch's Familiar (TV story)}}) The [[Metaltron]] claimed that Daleks did not fear. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Dalek (TV story)}}) However, the [[Cult of Skaro]] displayed fear of the [[Tenth Doctor]], physically recoiling at the mention of his name, ([[TV]]: {{cs|Doomsday (TV story)}}) and another [[Stone Dalek|Dalek]] begged [[River Song]] in terror for its life. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Big Bang (TV story)}}) The Daleks were also capable of anticipation, preferring to wait for their victims to run before exterminating them. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Magician's Apprentice (TV story)}}) The [[Twelfth Doctor]] believed that if a Dalek's [[cortex vault]] were to be deactivated, then it might be possible for a Dalek to experience a wider range of emotions. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Into the Dalek (TV story)}}) When discussing the comparatively less aggressive mindset of the Daleks who had fought in the [[Thal-Dalek battle]], the [[Seventh Doctor]] and [[Bernice Summerfield]] pondered that several centuries without victims to exterminate had allowed the Daleks' better nature to influence their attitudes. ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|The Lights of Skaro (audio story)}})

[[File:Renagade Dalek.jpg|thumb|right|A [[Renegade Dalek]]. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Remembrance of the Daleks (TV story)}})]]
According to the Tenth Doctor, Daleks were brilliant [[scientist]]s and [[engineer]]s. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Prisoner of the Daleks (novel)}}) According to [[K9 Mark II]]'s files, the Daleks' chief characteristics were "ruthlessness, cunning and implacable resolve". ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|The Dalek Contract (audio story)}}) [[Davros]] considered the Daleks to be single-minded, determined and ruthless. In the [[27th century]], [[Bernice Summerfield]] described the Daleks as "the most evil race the universe ever came up with". ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|The Lights of Skaro (audio story)}})

According to the [[Eleventh Doctor]], the Daleks were "the worst thing in all creation". They had "no conscience, no mercy [and] no pity". He claimed that "hate" looked like a Dalek and that "the Daleks [were] death". ([[TV]]: {{cs|Victory of the Daleks (TV story)}}) The [[Seventh Doctor]] declared the Daleks "irredeemably evil", although the [[Grey Man]] disagreed. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Falls the Shadow (novel)}}) While he originally thought there was no hope in the prospect, it was the [[Twelfth Doctor]]'s hope that he could turn [[Rusty (Into the Dalek)|Rusty]] "good", thereby opening the door to turn all Daleks into a force for good. However, he was saddened that Rusty instead simply redirected its hatred towards the Daleks. [[Journey Blue]] of the [[Combined Galactic Resistance]] said a Dalek was a raging lunatic. The Twelfth Doctor described the [[cortex vault]] stoking the fire of a Dalek's hate as "[[evil]] refined as [[engineering]]". ([[TV]]: {{cs|Into the Dalek (TV story)}})

The [[Sontaran Subliminal Education Matrix]]'s entry on the [[Dalek]]s acknowledged that they and the [[Sontaran]]s shared a [[bloodlust]] and a will to bend all opposition to their "iron rule", however, it maintained that the Sontarans were motivated by honour and their own "[[superiority]]" whilst the Daleks were motivated by their [[hatred]] for all other [[life form]]s which was characterised as a dishonourable "weakness" and "sickness" that dwarfed the Sontarans' own animosity for the [[Rutan]]s. It did, however, observe that the Daleks were "the right [[height]]". ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|A Soldier's Education (short story)}})

Daleks were prone to making blunt, absolute statements and would respond sincerely even to jestful comments. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Eve of the Daleks (TV story)}}) The [[Black Dalek Leader]] insisted that Daleks did not make [[mistake]]s. ([[TV]]: "[[Volcano (episode)|Volcano]]") [[Rusty (Into the Dalek)|Rusty]] believed that Daleks did not have [[soul]]s. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Into the Dalek (TV story)}}) One Dalek, after exterminating a group of fake [[singing]] Daleks, insisted that "Daleks do not sing." ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|Jubilee (audio story)}}) During the [[Planetary Relocation Incident]], a Dalek stated that Daleks did not accept [[apology|apologies]]. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Stolen Earth (TV story)}}) A [[Dalek (Prisoner of the Daleks)|Dalek prisoner]] claimed that Daleks did not [[capitulation|capitulate]] or [[plead]]. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Prisoner of the Daleks (novel)}}) A [[Defence Drone]] stated that the Daleks did not "make [[joke]]s". ([[TV]]: {{cs|Revolution of the Daleks (TV story)}}) Several [[Dalek Executioner]]s stated that Daleks were patient, supreme, unstoppable, "not fair", "not worried", and that they did not "store stuff" or have friends or managers. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Eve of the Daleks (TV story)}}) A [[Red Supreme Dalek (Liberation of the Daleks)|Red Supreme Dalek]] told [[Georgy Gold]] that Daleks did not [[plead]]. ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|Liberation of the Daleks (comic story)}})

=== Children of Davros ===
{{Section stub|Section should be expanded}}
[[File:DavrosJE1.jpg|right|thumb|Davros called himself the father of the Daleks. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Journey's End (TV story)}})]]
The Daleks were willing to kill their creator, Davros, on a number of occasions. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Genesis of the Daleks (TV story)}}, {{cs|Resurrection of the Daleks (TV story)}}) However, as recounted by [[Jack Harkness]], the Daleks repeatedly realised they needed their creator, specifically requiring his knowledge, genius, expertise, and creativity. ([[WC]]: {{cs|Monster File: Davros (webcast)}}) Davros stated that, thanks to a genetic defect he failed to remove, the Daleks showed [[respect]] and [[mercy]] towards him. This was why they allowed him to siphon their life energy to sustain himself while he was dying. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Witch's Familiar (TV story)}})

=== Religion ===
As noted above, the Daleks created by the manipulation and mutation of human genetic material by a demented [[Dalek Emperor]] were religious fanatics. They worshipped the Emperor as their god and even had a concept of blasphemy. Normal Daleks had no religion, other than their fanatic belief in their own supremacy, ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Parting of the Ways (TV story)}}) with some Daleks accordingly claiming there was no God. ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|The Final Phase (audio story)}}) However, two Dalek organisations, the [[Cult of Skaro]] and the [[Volatix Cabal]], did adopt names usually used to refer to religious groups. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Doomsday (TV story)}}, [[COMIC]]: {{cs|The Then and the Now (comic story)}})

=== Legal system ===
Although the Daleks had no regard for due process and [[galactic law]], there were a small number of occasions on which they took enemies back to Skaro for a "trial" rather than killing them on the spot. One such enemy was the [[renegade Time Lord]] known as [[the Master]], whose remains they even allowed the [[Eighth Doctor]] to collect and carry back to [[Gallifrey]]. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Doctor Who (TV story)}})

Another was their own creator, [[Davros]], whom they put on trial on several occasions. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Revelation of the Daleks (TV story)}}, [[COMIC]]: {{cs|Emperor of the Daleks! (comic story)}}, [[PROSE]]: {{cs|War of the Daleks (novel)}}, [[AUDIO]]: {{cs|I, Davros}}) Accounts differ as to whether some of these instances were "trials" in the criminal sense, ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|Emperor of the Daleks! (comic story)}}) a test to see if he was in fact worthy of becoming the supreme leader of the race, ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|I, Davros}}) or, to some extent, both at once. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|War of the Daleks (novel)}}

The Daleks on [[Vulcan (The Power of the Daleks)|Vulcan]] once referred to the precept of Daleks' supremacy of [[human]]s as "the Law of the Daleks", which they would have to "teach" to the human colonists when they made their move. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Power of the Daleks (TV story)}})

=== Dalek hierarchy ===
{{Main|Dalek hierarchy}}

Although they saw their entire species as superior, the Daleks had a hierarchical system. This included a wide range of ranks bestowed upon selected Daleks. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Dalek Invasion of Earth (TV story)}}, {{cs|The Evil of the Daleks (TV story)}}, {{cs|Victory of the Daleks (TV story)}})

=== Dalek writings ===
{{Main|Dalek writing}}

{{Main|Dalek (language)}}

The official language of the Daleks was simply known as [[Dalek (language)|Dalek]]. Swearwords existed in the language and were used to describe non-Dalek life forms, as they viewed them to be inferior species. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Twice Upon a Time (novelisation)}})

Daleks used inscriptions as recognition codes. They also measured time in [[rel]]s. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Doomsday (TV story)}}) They were able to read [[human]] numerals and words, even using them upon occasion. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Planet of the Daleks (TV story)}})

=== Names ===
In the early days of the Daleks' development on Skaro, some individual Daleks had actual [[name]]s, as evidenced by the scientist [[Zeg]]. ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|Duel of the Daleks (comic story)}}) One such Dalek was named [[DK3]]. ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|The Defeat of the Daleks (comic story)}}) However, by the time of the [[Dalek Emperor (The Evil of the Daleks)|Dalek Emperor]]'s scheme to isolate the [[Dalek factor]] and implant it in all of humanity, it was a mark of the [[Humanised Dalek]]s' oddness that they took on names — starting with [[Alpha (The Evil of the Daleks)|Alpha]], [[Beta (The Evil of the Daleks)|Beta]] and [[Omega (The Evil of the Daleks)|Omega]]. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Evil of the Daleks (TV story)}}) The [[Tenth Doctor]] later noted that the [[Cult of Skaro]]'s having names ([[Dalek Sec|Sec]], [[Dalek Thay|Thay]], [[Dalek Caan|Caan]] and [[Dalek Jast|Jast]]) was one of their unusual features. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Doomsday (TV story)}})

The [[Eleventh Doctor]] made reference to "[[Bob the Nasty Dalek]]" while speaking about [[Last Great Time War|Time War]] combatants. ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|The Then and the Now (comic story)}}) In place of names, Dalek soldiers could be designated with a [[number]] by their superiors; the newly-created Daleks on [[Vulcan (The Power of the Daleks)|Vulcan]] were referred to by the original three by designations such as "[[Dalek 9 (The Power of the Daleks)|Dalek 9]]" and "[[Dalek 10 (The Power of the Daleks)|Dalek 10]]". ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Power of the Daleks (TV story)}}) Daleks also referred to each other as such during their invasion of [[Trodos]], ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|The Trodos Ambush (comic story)}}) and one one of the Daleks participating in the conquest of [[Planet (The Defeat of the Daleks)|another planet]] was known as [[DK3]]. ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|The Defeat of the Daleks (comic story)}})

Several other Daleks throughout history were granted names, not by themselves, but by [[the Doctor]] — including [[Dal (Echoes of War)|Dal]], ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|Echoes of War (audio story)}}) [[Rusty (Into the Dalek)|Rusty]], ([[TV]]: {{cs|Into the Dalek (TV story)}}, {{cs|Twice Upon a Time (TV story)}}) and [[Lumpy]]. ([[GAME]]: {{cs|The Doctor and the Dalek (video game)}}) The [[Space Security Service]] also assigned numbers to captured Daleks. ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|The Only Good Dalek (comic story)}})

=== Cultural effect ===
{{main|Daleks in popular culture and mythology}}

[[File:Thought Channel.jpg|thumb|The Second Doctor shows the Time Lords a mental projection of the Daleks. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The War Games (TV story)}})]]
The Daleks had a devastating effect on the races and individuals that encountered them. For the most part they epitomised fear and danger, especially for [[the Doctor]], who in their [[Eleventh Doctor|eleventh incarnation]] considered them to be his "enemy", and him theirs; ([[TV]]: {{cs|Victory of the Daleks (TV story)}}) upon arriving in [[1966]] and seeing the [[Post Office Tower]] that contained [[WOTAN]], the [[First Doctor]] remarked to [[Dodo Chaplet|Dodo]] he had felt like that when the Daleks were near. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The War Machines (TV story)}}) The [[Second Doctor]] used his encounters with them to warn [[Zoe Heriot]] of what she might encounter. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Wheel in Space (TV story)}}) The Second Doctor also later used a mental projection of a Dalek to show the [[Time Lord]]s of his enemies. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The War Games (TV story)}}) A Dalek was one of many fears that assaulted the [[Third Doctor]] in the [[Keller Machine]]. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Mind of Evil (TV story)}})

When he approached his fourth regeneration, a vision of [[Dalek leader (Destiny of the Daleks)|a Dalek]] came to the [[Fourth Doctor]]. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Logopolis (TV story)}}) An [[Amnesia|amnesic]] [[Eighth Doctor]] once looked suspiciously at a pepper pot, which was similar to a Dalek's shape. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|The City of the Dead (novel)}}) The Eighth Doctor also described the Daleks as "the greatest threat this universe has ever seen." ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|Blood of the Daleks (audio story)}}) Their power over the Doctor continued through his personality when he used a [[Chameleon Arch]]; his human self, [[John Smith (Tenth Doctor)|John Smith]], sketched a Dalek within his [[A Journal of Impossible Things (Human Nature)|Journal of Impossible Things]]. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Human Nature (TV story)}})

Daleks were among the creatures in the [[Atraxi]]'s files of races that invaded Earth. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Eleventh Hour (TV story)}}) Survivors of the [[22nd century Dalek invasion]] took to calling them "the Invaders." ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|A Star's View of Caroline (short story)}}) The Fourth Doctor knew that "It's just one Dalek" were famous last words, claiming that countless civilisations had fallen to single Daleks. ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|Genetics of the Daleks (audio story)}})

Their danger was on occasion negligible compared to a greater threat; when speaking of his fellow Time Lords at his trial, the [[Sixth Doctor]] stated that the Daleks were "still in the nursery" compared to them. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Ultimate Foe (TV story)}}) When [[Rassilon]] threatened to break the [[time lock]] on the [[Last Great Time War]] the [[Tenth Doctor]] warned {{Simm}}, that "not just the Daleks" would be unleashed if it were broken. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The End of Time (TV story)}}) Nonetheless, when the Doctors united to [[Fall of Gallifrey|save Gallifrey]] at the end of the War, they were concerned with the threat of the Daleks above any other danger. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Day of the Doctor (TV story)}})

[[File:Kodath Squadron.jpg|left|thumb|A human is horrified by the mere appearance of [[Kodath Squadron]]. ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|Children of the Revolution (comic story)}})]]
The Daleks' impact on those [[human]]s who encountered them had different effects on their psyches. They appeared in dreams or visions; [[Ace]] associated the Daleks with [[Nazi]]s; a Dalek with a swastika chased her, chanting "Heil Doktor" following her time in an alternate universe populated by Nazis. ([[PROSE]]: ''[[Timewyrm: Exodus (novel)|Timewyrm: Exodus]]'') She later called the Daleks "the catch" to [[Companion|travelling with]] the Doctor. ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|Enemy of the Daleks (audio story)}}) To [[Bernice Summerfield]], [[Dalek (The Also People)|a Dalek]] appeared in a dream, alongside several other beings such as the [[Sontaran]] [[Grinx]] and [[Cyberman (The Also People)|a Cyberman]], in which the nature of [[evil]] was dissected. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|The Also People (novel)}}) [[Sam Jones]], on awakening from unconsciousness exclaimed, "Anyone get the number of that Dalek?". ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|The Taint (novel)}}) Upon seeing an inert Dalek in [[UNIT]]'s collection, [[Cleo Proctor]] felt deeply afraid, even though she did not know why. ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|Recruits (audio story)}})

Alternatively, encounters with the Daleks took a certain pride of place for some individuals. [[Rose Tyler]] and [[Sarah Jane Smith]] compared their experiences encountering Daleks, and, in Rose's case, the [[Dalek Emperor in the Last Great Time War|Dalek Emperor]], upon meeting, ([[TV]]: {{cs|School Reunion (TV story)}}) yet both were terrified, deep down, of the exterminators, with Rose even warning [[Jackie Tyler|her mother]] of them. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Doomsday (TV story)}}, {{cs|The Stolen Earth (TV story)}}) During the 2009 invasion, upon hearing the transmission of "EXTERMINATE", Sarah Jane and [[Jack Harkness]] reacted with undiluted terror, crying and holding their loved ones close. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Stolen Earth (TV story)}}) The Doctor's friend [[Winston Churchill]] originally saw the [[Ironside Project|Ironsides]] as "our salvation" and as a weapon to use to destroy the [[Third Reich]] and for the [[Allies (World War II)|Allies]] to win [[World War II]] due to their hostility. When the [[Eleventh Doctor]] attacked them with a spanner, Winston described the "machines" as "precious", only to then learn of the Daleks' true nature and watch as they murdered two [[marine]]s. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Victory of the Daleks (TV story)}})

Although most of the humans on the frontier world of [[Red Rocket Rising]] forgot about the Daleks, to the point where Acting President [[Eileen Klint]] initially believed them to be pitied and not feared, [[Tom Cardwell]] recognised them from the old records as "the worst of them all", and tried urging the other humans to run for the hills. ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|Blood of the Daleks (audio story)}}) The Sontarans knew of how dangerous the Daleks where and, if a single Dalek were to make its way to [[Sontar]], [[Major]] [[Skar]] was prepared to put his armies on high alert. ([[GAME]]: {{cs|The Doctor and the Dalek (video game)}}) The Time Lords thought similarly, understanding that a single [[Dalek drone]] would be all it took to bring down [[Arcadia (city)|Arcadia]]. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Last Day (TV story)}})

When [[Chris Cwej]] went to Skaro to negotiate with the Daleks during the [[War in Heaven]], he was horrified to be dealing with the greatest threat to life in the universe. After his discussions with them, he was left in a state of horrified shock and was questioning his humanity, having [[sex]] with [[Christine Summerfield]] in an desperate attempt to regain the feeling of being human. In ''[[Dead Romance]]'', Christine called the Daleks the "machine people" and dedicated the book to them, ignoring the fact that they were mass-murders to instead focus on how they had survived the Time Lords trying to wipe them out. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Dead Romance (novel)}}) The [[Testimony Foundation]], a organisation that existed during the era of [[New Earth]], knew of the Daleks and Davros. Encounters between the Doctor and the Daleks were among the events they showcased when confronting his [[First Doctor|First]] and [[Twelfth Doctor|Twelfth]] incarnations. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Twice Upon a Time (TV story)}})

== Dalek technology ==
=== Overview ===
[[File:Transolar Disks.jpg|thumb|The Daleks flew on [[hoverbout]]s throughout their history. ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|Fire and Brimstone (comic story)}})]]
The key item of Dalek technology was the casing, derived from the Mark III Travel Machines built by [[Davros]]. The casings of Davros' [[Imperial Dalek]]s were made out of bonded [[polycarbide]]. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Remembrance of the Daleks (TV story)}})

The [[Dalek eyestalk|eyestalk]] of the casing bestowed superior vision to the Dalek creature. The plunger-shaped attachment functioned as a flexible and adaptable limb. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Dalek (TV story)}})

The [[Contagium]] was a wasp-like machine that produced [[nanite]]s within a victim, infecting their [[brain]] to turn them into a Dalek slave. ([[COMIC]]: {{cs|Fire and Brimstone (comic story)}}) On the [[Dalek Asylum]] there was a [[nanocloud]] virus that physically transformed organisms into [[Dalek puppet]]s which removed all emotion except anger and hatred. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Asylum of the Daleks (TV story)}})

On the surface of Skaro, within the confines of the Dalek City, the machines ran on [[static electricity]] fed from the city floor. They were incapacitated if removed from the floor. The casing technology changed over the years. The first Daleks to emerge from the bunker in which they had been entombed built a city and power from those. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Daleks (TV story)}}) Those occupying Earth during the [[2150s Dalek invasion of Earth|their 22nd century invasion]] had dishes on their backs. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Dalek Invasion of Earth (TV story)}}) Later models of Dalek casing had internal power supplies, and even [[repulsor]] system ([[AUDIO]]: ''[[The Enemy of My Enemy (audio story)|The Enemy of My Enemy]]'') that allowed them to hover ([[TV]]: {{cs|Remembrance of the Daleks (TV story)}}, {{cs|Dalek (TV story)}}) and fly. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Parting of the Ways (TV story)}}, {{cs|Army of Ghosts (TV story)}}/{{cs|Doomsday (TV story)}}, {{cs|The Stolen Earth (TV story)}}/{{cs|Journey's End (TV story)}})

Throughout time and space, there were many [[Dalek variants]] that sported different casings. A Dalek's ability depended on what features its casing offered. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Daleks (TV story)}}, {{cs|The Evil of the Daleks (TV story)}}) The default manipulator arm could be replaced with the likes of flamethrowers and seismic detectors. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Chase (TV story)}}, {{cs|The Daleks' Master Plan (TV story)}})

[[File:Bastic bullets.jpg|left|thumb|Using their [[force field]]s, the Daleks were protected from various attacks, even [[bastic bullet]]s. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Parting of the Ways (TV story)}})]]
By the era of the [[Last Great Time War]], Daleks had force-fields. Whereas previous versions of Daleks could be destroyed by a well-placed [[bastic bullet]], such bullets could not get close to these Daleks' casings. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Dalek (TV story)}}, {{cs|The Parting of the Ways (TV story)}}) However, they could be penetrated by their own weaponry, and variations thereof. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Evolution of the Daleks (TV story)}}, {{cs|Victory of the Daleks (TV story)}}) They not only could hover, but travel independently through space. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Parting of the Ways (TV story)}}) If an individual touched the casing, they could be burned alive. These Daleks could also use the [[DNA]] of a [[time travel]]ler to regenerate their bodies just by virtue of the traveller touching the casing. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Dalek (TV story)}})

The Daleks were also experts in biological warfare, and used (or attempted to use) biological weapons on several occasions. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Dalek Invasion of Earth (TV story)}}, {{cs|Planet of the Daleks (TV story)}}, {{cs|Death to the Daleks (TV story)}})

Dalek travel technology varied over time. Dalek spaceships were (almost) consistently designed in a [[Dalek flying saucer|saucer shape]], ([[TV]]: {{cs|Bad Wolf (TV story)}}/{{cs|The Parting of the Ways (TV story)}}, {{cs|The Stolen Earth (TV story)}}/{{cs|Journey's End (TV story)}}, {{cs|Victory of the Daleks (TV story)}}) and [[hoverbout]]s allowed individual Daleks to travel without using their own power. ([[AUDIO]]: ''[[Fugitives (audio story)|Fugitives]]'') The Daleks could apply [[dimensional transcendentalism]] to their ships and had their own version of the [[chameleon circuit]]. ([[AUDIO]]: {{cs|The Apocalypse Element (audio story)}}) They were also able to hack into [[virtual reality]] systems, creating attack ships in [[Puterspace]], although they were not particularly good at it. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Love and War (novel)}})

[[File:Progenitor Daleks Time Corridor.jpg|right|thumb|[[Dalek ship (Victory of the Daleks)|A Dalek flying saucer]] uses a [[time corridor]] to travel in time. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Victory of the Daleks (TV story)}})]]
The Daleks also developed time travel capabilities, usually in the form of [[time corridor]]s which allowed limited transport between one era and another. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Resurrection of the Daleks (TV story)}}) The Daleks also developed [[Dalek time machine|their own kind of time machine]] of similar capacities to [[the Doctor's TARDIS]]; though they could not change shape, they were also dimensionally transcendental. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Chase (TV story)}}, {{cs|The Daleks' Master Plan (TV story)}}) Members of the [[Cult of Skaro]] could initiate 'emergency [[temporal shift]]s', which acted as teleports through time and space to let the Dalek escape a threat. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Doomsday (TV story)}}, {{cs|Daleks in Manhattan (TV story)}}, {{cs|The Stolen Earth (TV story)}})

=== Dalek weaponry ===
{{Main|Dalek weaponry}}
Dalek [[gunstick]]s could kill almost any sentient being ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Daleks (TV story)}}, et al.) and could paralyse their victims temporarily or permanently. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Daleks (TV story)|namedpart=The Survivors (2)}})

[[File:Dalekgun.jpg|thumb|left|A Dalek fires its death ray. ([[TV]]: {{cs|Dalek (TV story)}})]]
The Daleks' gunstick evolved alongside other aspects of Dalek technology. Daleks could also change the effects of their guns' energy projectiles; at the lowest level, they would merely temporarily disable an individual in the area the projectiles struck. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Daleks (TV story)}}) The highest setting on a Dalek gunstick would reduce a human to atoms, but the Daleks rarely used that. Instead, they made certain to dial their guns down to the lowest possible setting that would kill a person - that way, Daleks would ensure that all of their victims died as slowly and painfully as possible. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Prisoner of the Daleks (novel)}}) Indeed, it had been the goal of [[Scientist Dalek]]s to ensure their gunsticks did not simply kill victims, but "exterminate" them. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Dalek (novelisation)}})

Instead of simply destroying worlds from orbit, as their starships often could, ([[TV]]: {{cs|Asylum of the Daleks (TV story)}}) the Daleks thus waged large-scale invasions on most occasions, shooting their victims with their gunsticks ([[GAME]]: {{cs|City of the Daleks (video game)}}, [[COMIC]]: {{cs|Liberation of the Daleks (comic story)}}) and therefore making non-Dalek species die in pain. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Prisoner of the Daleks (novel)}}, {{cs|Dalek (novelisation)}}) The survival of a planet also allowed the Daleks to mine its resources. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Engines of War (novel)}})

The Dalek gunstick and [[manipulator arm]] could be re-purposed depending on what task was likely to face a specific individual, or removed altogether to render them defenceless and prevent mad Daleks from turning on them, particularly the ones in the intensive care in the [[Dalek Asylum]]. The alternatives were far ranging in the different functions they performed. ([[TV]]: {{cs|The Chase (TV story)}}, {{cs|The Parting of the Ways (TV story)}}, {{cs|Asylum of the Daleks (TV story)}})

As showcased by [[Rusty (Into the Dalek)|Rusty]] on [[Villengard]], a Dalek could also detach a gunstick from its casing, effectively able to throw the weapon a short distance. However, the Daleks were also [[telekinesis|telekinetic]] in some respect; the mutant would be able to recall the thrown blaster to its casing in a few short moments. ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Twice Upon a Time (novelisation)}})

== Behind the scenes ==
=== Other appearances ===
[[File:Doctor Who Worlds of Wonder Dalek (Scotland).jpeg|thumb|right|A Dalek on display for [[Doctor Who Worlds of Wonder]]]]
Two ''Doctor Who'' movies starring [[Peter Cushing]] featured the Daleks as the main villains: ''[[Dr. Who and the Daleks (theatrical film)|Dr. Who and the Daleks]]'', and ''[[Daleks' Invasion Earth 2150 A.D. (theatrical film)|Daleks' Invasion Earth 2150 A.D.]]'', based loosely on the television serials ''The Daleks'' and ''The Dalek Invasion of Earth'' respectively. However, this wiki only considers the original televised stories by [[Terry Nation]] as [[valid source]]s. The movies used brand new Dalek props, based closely on the original design but with a wider range of colours. Originally, the movie Daleks were supposed to shoot jets of flame, but this was thought to be too graphic for children, so their weapons emitted jets of deadly vapour instead. They also appeared in the ''Doctor Who'' Comic Relief parody, {{cs|The Curse of Fatal Death (TV story)}}.

One of the visions of his future the [[Eighth Doctor]] saw in {{cs|Father Time (novel)}} was a Dalek, foreshadowing that one of the upcoming [[BBC Eighth Doctor Adventures]] was supposed to feature them. This foreshadowing ([[PROSE]]: {{cs|Father Time (novel)}}) would have been payed off in {{cs|Sometime Never... (novel)}}, as [[Sabbath Dei]]'s allies were supposed to be the Daleks. However, copyright stopped this from happening. ([[DWM 341]]) Test pages for a possible [[Twelfth Doctor]] Dalek comic were drawn by [[Brian Williamson]] for [[Titan Publishing Group]]. However, Titan would only manage to debut the proper Dalek design in its comics in ''[[Time Lord Victorious]]''. <ref>https://downthetubes.net/daleks-debut-at-last-in-titan-comics-doctor-who-time-lord-victorious-tie-in/</ref>

Outside of ''Doctor Who'', Daleks also made an appearance in the film ''Looney Tunes: Back in Action'' and the ''[[Star Wars]]'' comic strip, ''Fett Club''. A Dalek-based Transformer named [https://tfwiki.net/wiki/Octus_(G1) Octus] that would transform into a Mark III Travel Machine features in an issue of Marvel UK's ''Transformers'' comic, as well as the Decepticon Starscream picking up Dalek transmissions while flying over a field in [[England]]. Spike Milligan wrote a sketch which featured a working-class Dalek with a family of his own, and a Dalek-spoof race (known as the Deacons) made an appearance in a ''Futurama'' comic.

=== Story titles ===
Beginning with the 1965 stage play ''[[The Curse of the Daleks (stage play)|The Curse of the Daleks]]'', the best-known title format for stories featuring the Daleks has been "... of the Daleks". This was first used on television in the 1966 serial {{cs|The Power of the Daleks (TV story)}} and was used most recently on TV in 2022's {{cs|Eve of the Daleks (TV story)}}. In fact, if comic strips, audios and novels are included, more stories exist that do ''not'' use this title format, but "... of the Daleks" is considered ubiquitous enough that the spoof film ''[[Myth Runner (home video)|Myth Runner]]'' includes a joking reference to an apparent future Who story entitled ''Deuteronomy of the Daleks''.

The word ''Dalek'' has been titular to more ''Doctor Who'' televised ''story'' titles than any other noun, although ''Planet'' and ''Death'' are more ubiquitous if [[William Hartnell|Hartnell]]-era adventures — which originally did not have story titles as such — are identified only by their episodic titles. Indeed, in the whole of the Hartnell era, ''Dalek'' was used exactly once as an onscreen title — for episode two of the adventure later re-christened as {{cs|The Dalek Invasion of Earth (TV story)}}, "{{cs|The Daleks (episode)}}".

=== A Nazi by any other name ===
As he grew up during [[World War II]], Terry Nation had vivid memories of the war and, in particular, the [[Nazi]]s. The Daleks share many characteristics with the Nazi party deliberately. They both believe in the superiority of their race, whether it means the entire species, like the Daleks, or their ethnicity, like the [[Germany|German]] Nazis. {{cs|Genesis of the Daleks (TV story)}} is the most clear depiction of this parallel, with the Kaleds showing dedication to their cause and near-complete conformity. It also showed the killing of any opposed to their ideology; in this case, the Kaled scientists. Their shrieking voices were designed to parody the loud repetitive chanting and rants associated with Nazi rallies. The casting out or forced labour of the [[Muto]]s is comparable to the [[Holocaust]], as is the Kaled consensus of them as lesser beings. Another comparison to the Holocaust appears in {{cs|The Dalek Invasion of Earth (TV story)}}, in which Daleks refer to the destruction of Earth as "the final solution", a phrase associated with Nazism. They even greet each other by raising their plungers vertically in a way reminiscent of the Nazi salute. Another blatant reference appears in {{cs|Journey's End (TV story)}} with Daleks chanting "Exterminieren!" as they invade Germany. {{cs|Just War (novel)}} and {{cs|Daleks Among Us (audio story)}} more explicity highlight the parallels and similarities between the Nazis and the Daleks.

Contrariwise, other writers have pointed out the flaws in comparing the Daleks to the Nazis. [[John Peel]] noted in the introduction to ''[[The Official Doctor Who & the Daleks Book]]'':

{{Quote|They have been compared over the years with Nazis, but this is a tenuous connection at best. Certainly there is a lack of individuality, an unquestioning obedience of orders and a willingness to die for the race - all of this epitomised the Nazi stormtrooper ideal. It isn't hard to see, though, even in the most evil member of the Nazi hierarchy, some spark of buried humanity. Even the elite had their fears and superstitions. The Daleks had none of these.|[[John Peel]]|The Official Doctor Who & the Daleks Book}}

In ''[[AHistory]]'', [[Lance Parkin]] expands on this idea:

{{Quote|Real life analogies quickly fail when applied to the Daleks. At times they're compared to the likes of Nazis, but in truth they're literally lacking in humanity. Even "conquest" as we generally understand the term doesn't really interest them - sometimes they put foes to work as slaves (as in ''Death to the Daleks''), but this is almost inevitably in the interest of facilitating new atrocities and exterminations. The point is that one can (and should) hope to use reason against real-world governments, but there is virtually no chance of diplomacy succeeding against the Daleks. ... Basically, the Daleks collectively remain united behind one goal: kill everything that isn't a Dalek.|[[Lance Parkin]]|aHistory}}

=== The catchphrase ===
The single word most associated with the Daleks is "''Exterminate!''", which has been uttered by generations of British children impersonating the creatures. However, although a variant of the word, "exterminated", can be heard from the very first appearance of the Daleks, it was not until the final episode ({{cs|Flashpoint (episode)}}) of their second story arc, [[TV]]: {{cs|The Dalek Invasion of Earth (TV story)}}, that a Dalek finally was heard uttering the word "''Exterminate!''"

This was referenced in {{cs|Return to Skaro (audio story)}}, a direct sequel to ''The Daleks'', in which the First Doctor states that he remembers the Daleks using the word "extermination" during his previous encounter. He claims the word "fits so easily on the Daleks tongue."

=== Design ===
When ''Doctor Who'' was about to return in the mid-2000s, re-imagining how the Daleks would look was a hotly pursued job. On his first day as ''Doctor Who'' production designer, in 2004, one of the earliest tasks [[Ed Thomas]] had was to select art department staff members from a stack of portfolios on his desk, about which he later noted, "Everyone who had ever drawn a Dalek in their entire life had sent in their CV." The assignment of redesigning the aliens was ultimately given to [[Matt Savage]], with whom Thomas watched ''The Dalek Invasion of Earth'' on Savage's very first morning of employment on the series. He remembered, "Ed said: 'We'd like you to spruce up the Daleks.' I was a massive fan. I couldn't believe it. I was grinning from ear to ear." Savage was thereafter instrumental to the redesign of the Daleks' exterior casing. "I put rivets everywhere and some text under the eyestalk, which was like their barcode," he said. (''ImageFX'' magazine, October 2008, pp. 61 & 62)

=== Music ===
In the [[BBC Wales]] version, [[Murray Gold]] has given the Daleks multiple leitmotifs, with the first being in the form of the track identified as "[[The Daleks (Dalek song)|The Daleks]]" on ''[[Doctor Who - Series 1 and 2 (soundtrack)|Doctor Who - Series 1 and 2]]''. This track was heavily choral and the operatic elements were recorded with the [[Crouch End Festival Chorus]] in early 2005 at AIR Studios, London. The [[Doctor Who Confidential|Confidential]] for the series 1 episode "{{cs|Dalek (TV story)}}" features a segment that shows the choir recordings taking place, as well as an interview with Murray Gold. Later Dalek music also continues the choral presence, with "[[Evolution of the Daleks (song)|Evolution of the Daleks]]" and "[[The Dark and Endless Dalek Night]]" containing similar chanting. In all of Murray Gold's Dalek leitmotifs, [[:Hebrew#Behind the scenes|the lyrics are in Hebrew]].

=== Cameos ===


Due to the popularity of ''Doctor Who'', Daleks feature briefly in many other shows, movies, and popular culture. In ''The Simpsons'' episode "Holidays of Future Passed", for example, a blue Dalek briefly chases a woman in and out of a revolving door at the "Benny Hilton" Hotel, accompanied by the theme song from the ''Benny Hill Show''.

In the comedy film ''Looney Tunes: Back in Action'', the characters visit "Area 52", a government facility where numerous extraterrestrials (most of them modelled after 1960's theatrical and televisual aliens) are held. Among the most prominent are two Daleks (in a design based on the alternate-continuity film ''[[Dr. Who and the Daleks (theatrical film)|Dr. Who and the Daleks]]''), who join the other aliens in trying to attack the protagonists, but end up blasting each other instead as their quarries escape.

In the [[David Walliams]] novel ''Grandpa's Great Ecscape'', kids dress up as Daleks, along with [[Cyberman|Cybermen]] and [[Sontaran]]s, using costumes stolen from a [[Doctor Who exhibition|''Doctor Who'' exhibition]], and pretend that there is an [[alien invasion]] of Earth.

In the game ''LEGO Dimensions'', they act as enemies who serve Lord Vortech. Their design is different due to the greyish colour casing and golden eye stalk (while the physical figurine is the exact colour). Other Daleks have appeared such as the Emperor and Rusty. In the ''Lego Batman Movie'' story mode, they replace the paradigm Daleks and have different built fenders.

In ''The LEGO Batman Movie'', a number of Daleks, coloured according to the [[New Dalek Paradigm]], can be seen among the inhabitants of the Phantom Zone, alongside many famous villains from a number of fictional franchises. Like the others, they are unleashed upon Gotham City by the supervillain known as "the Joker" at the climax of the film, only to be defeated and sealed back inside the prison dimension. Archive audio of [[Nicholas Briggs]] exclaiming "Exterminate!" from {{cs|The Parting of the Ways (TV story)}} is used.

A Dalek appears in the movie ''Ted 2'', where it fought Robby the Robot.

In the Online Game Overwatch, Bastion, a robotic character have a voiceline meant to immitate the Dalek's "Exterminate" catchphrase. Bastion in question being a robotic war machine from a bygone war of human extermination.

=== Invalid sources ===
''[[The Discontinuity Guide]]'' made the claim that, originally, [[Davros]] was killed and forgotten, and that the [[Fourth Doctor]]'s [[Genesis Incident|interference with the creation of the Daleks]] created a new [[timeline]] where Davros survived, the Doctor's warnings about the Daleks having made Davros paranoid enough to activate a [[force field]] in his chair. As a result, whilst the Daleks originally had a solid, cohesive [[Dalek Empire|empire]], always with one purpose, Davros' presence reduced them to "a mess of squabbling factions" which were "incapable of the unity needed to develop [[Dimensional transcendentalism|dimensionally transcendental]] [[time travel]]. Published before the [[Last Great Time War]] was established in ''Doctor Who'' lore, ''The Discontinuity Guide'' went on to claim that "whilst Davros lives the Daleks will remain disorganised, and will never become the threat that the Time Lords so feared."<ref>[http://www.bbc.co.uk/doctorwho/classic/episodeguide/dalekhistory2.shtml BBC.co.uk 'Discontinuity Guide' article on '''Dalek History: Part Two''' in the original series of ''Doctor Who'']</ref>

The Daleks were responsible for the destruction of [[Daxus]] and the genocide of nearly all [[Dax]] in ''[[The Corinthian Project (novel)|The Corinthian Project]]''.
